summary:
Poland does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct: the 1932 Penal Code decriminalised it with an equal age of consent of 15, reaffirmed in 1948, and homosexuality was removed from the disease list in 1991. The current legal framework nonetheless leaves trans visitors exposed in several documented ways.

Legal gender recognition exists but is procedurally demanding. A trans person must obtain a medical diagnosis and undergo hormone replacement therapy before legal gender change; such changes have been performed since the 1960s. Because any surgery resulting in infertility is prohibited under Penal Code art. 156 §1 (with narrow medical exceptions such as uterine cancer), castration on request is illegal, so a trans person must change legal gender before sex reassignment surgery can proceed. Until March 2025 the process required litigation against one's own parents; on 4 March 2025 the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court resolved that recognition should proceed as a non-trial vital-records rectification on request alone, with the spouse as the only possible other participant and immediate effect upon positive review. A 2015 Sejm bill that would have allowed recognition without physical intervention was vetoed by President Duda in October 2015 and the veto was not overridden.

Detention and prison practice have endangered trans detainees' health. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after NGO intervention the Border Guard commander ordered her release, but her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused to supply medication. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy and ordered EUR 8,000 in damages, establishing that trans prisoners can litigate medication denial successfully.

Hate-crime and hate-speech law does not currently cover gender identity or sexual orientation. Poland's existing hate-crime law punishes bias-motivated violence, threats, insults and promotion of hateful ideologies only where motivated by national, ethnic, racial, political or religious affiliation. Parliament passed an amendment on 6 March 2025 adding sexual orientation and sex or gender, with up to three years' imprisonment for insulting or inciting hatred; President Andrzej Duda declined to sign it on 17 April 2025 and referred it for constitutional review on free-expression grounds. A parallel Penal Code amendment adopted by parliament in March 2025 was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal by President Duda in April 2025 and ruled unconstitutional on 30 September 2025, so the extended protections, including gender, never entered into force. The Prosecutor General has set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement, and a Deputy Justice Minister announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, but approval of the draft was postponed.

Marriage is constitutionally limited to opposite-sex couples under Article 18, and there is no general recognition of same-sex couples beyond limited rights of shared tenancy, refusal to testify as the closest person under Penal Code Article 115(11), and EU-law residency. On 20 March 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled registries must recognise and transcribe marriage certificates of same-sex couples married in another EU member state, first implemented in Warsaw on 14 May 2026; on 28 July 2026 the Constitutional Tribunal ruled such transcription incompatible with the Constitution. On 29 May 2026 the Sejm passed the Act on the Status of the Closest Person granting limited notarised cohabitation rights, pending Senate and presidential approval opposed by President Karol Nawrocki. In September 2024 the ECtHR ruled that Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an 'illegal vacuum' violating their rights and called for a recognition framework; in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad. LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government has been assessed as slow and insufficient.

Openly transgender people are officially barred from military service on medical grounds: a diagnosis of gender dysphoria results in automatic assignment as permanently and completely unfit for service in both conflict and peace. In February 2025 the Supreme Court ruled that a non-binary casino dealer in Wrocław dismissed in 2021 for refusing female appearance rules requiring make-up, skirts and high heels had suffered gender-based discrimination, the first explicit recognition under Polish law that non-binary persons can face gender discrimination.

Anti-LGBT resolutions have been largely cleared from legal circulation. On 6 February 2024 the Warsaw Voivodeship Administrative Court annulled the March 2019 Mordy commune resolution against 'LGBT ideology', the last explicit anti-LGBT resolution, after administrative courts including the Supreme Administrative Court in June 2022 held such resolutions exceeded council powers, grossly breached the Constitution, and violated the dignity, honour, reputation and private life of LGBT residents. Eleven similar discriminatory acts remain in force, including 10 Ordo Iuris Family Rights Charters in named counties, communes and cities; most other councils repealed theirs under EU partnership conditionality barring EU support to authorities contributing to segregation or exclusion.

Documented hostility includes President Duda's 2020 election statement that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism', Gazeta Polska's distribution of 'LGBT-free zone' stickers later reworded after a court halted distribution, and a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 where the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland. On 20 July 2019 the first Equality March in Białystok with about 800 marchers was confronted by more than 4,000 counter-protesters throwing stones, bricks, firecrackers, flash bombs, rotten eggs and bottles filled with urine, requiring heavy riot police intervention. On 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest, some peacefully protesting activist Margot's arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman. Amnesty International's 2025 report 'A Thousand Cuts' documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, against the legacy of LGBT-free zones from 2019-23; X removed its misgendering and deadnaming rule in April 2023 and reinstated it in 2024.

The 2019 EU LGBTI Survey II found 1 in 5 trans and intersex people in Poland were physically or sexually attacked in the five years before the survey; this figure is a survey snapshot from 2019, not a current rate. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory for Poland lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days.
tangentialFactors:
Poland's administrative regime for transgender persons operates under the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act; scholarly legal analysis in Przegląd Sejmowy 2024/5 examines whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, particularly on civil status.

Historical precedent for state-led censorship exists: in March 2007 the then government proposed fast-track legislation punishing anyone who promoted homosexuality in schools with dismissal, fines or prison, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with a deputy minister announcing teachers who revealed homosexuality would be fired. Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, and 'pink files' were still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005 despite activists' requests to destroy them.

ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries. After 2015 several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones', partly in response to mayor Rafał Trzaskowski's pro-LGBT declaration. At a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland.

Support infrastructure includes the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), and Lambda, registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990. The first sex reassignment surgery in Poland was performed in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie, and the first recorded transgender meeting took place on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology. Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe.

Homophobia is described as a common public attitude driven by Catholic Church influence and widespread social conservatism; the Church influenced the 1988 blocking of the Warsaw Gay Movement's legal registration, and in August 2020 the Episcopal Conference recommended counselling centres to help regain natural sexual orientation, dismissing scientific consensus on the ineffectiveness and harm of conversion therapy as political correctness.

Openly transgender Poles are officially barred from military service on medical grounds: a gender dysphoria diagnosis results in automatic assignment as permanently and completely unfit for service in both conflict and peace.

Anti-discrimination protections are limited. The Labour Code has banned employment discrimination based on sexual orientation since 2003, and the equal-treatment law in force from 1 January 2011 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment only. In 2019 the Constitutional Tribunal found unconstitutional the Petty Offence Code provision punishing denial of goods and services without just cause, after the Supreme Court in 2018 had found a Łódź printer acted illegally in refusing banners for an LGBT group. Hate-crime and hate-speech law does not cover sexual orientation, sex or gender, or gender identity: the 6 March 2025 amendment adding these grounds was unsigned by President Duda on 17 April 2025 and the parallel amendment was ruled unconstitutional by the Constitutional Tribunal on 30 September 2025.

A registered-partnership bill without joint adoption was added to the Sejm agenda on 8 July 2024 after its October 2024 presentation by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula; on 29 May 2026 the Sejm passed the Act on the Status of the Closest Person granting limited notarised cohabitation rights, pending Senate and presidential approval opposed by President Karol Nawrocki.

A February 2019 draft bill to ban conversion therapy was submitted by MPs but no ban is in force.

In February 2025 the Supreme Court recognised gender-based discrimination against a non-binary casino dealer in Wrocław dismissed in 2021 for refusing female appearance rules, the first explicit recognition under Polish law that non-binary persons can face gender discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:

Whether the Act on the Status of the Closest Person passed by the Sejm on 29 May 2026 has cleared Senate and presidential approval is unresolved in this record; the source notes President Karol Nawrocki's opposition.

Whether the hate-speech and hate-crime amendments referred to the Constitutional Tribunal will be retabled after the 30 September 2025 ruling is not sourced here.

The Association for Legal Intervention case of March 2024 documents a trans detainee's hormone therapy being interrupted for three months; whether comparable incidents have occurred since is unresolved in this record, and the most recent documented instance of this specific harm is from March 2024.

No trans-specific killing or violence rate for Poland with a denominator and period appears in this inventory, so no comparative magnitude can be stated.
